claim: WDR5 is a highly conserved protein that moonlights in a variety of functions in the nucleus.
source: WDR5 is a highly conserved protein that moonlights in a variety of functions in the nucleus.
evidence: This is a general statement about WDR5 that draws from established scientific knowledge about the protein's characteristics and functions.

claim: WDR5 rose to prominence as a component of epigenetic writer complexes that deposit histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methylation.
source: It rose to prominence as a component of epigenetic writer complexes that deposit histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methylation (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018.

claim: WDR5 acts outside epigenetic writer complexes to facilitate the integrity of the mitotic spindle.
source: but was subsequently found to act outside these complexes to facilitate the integrity of the mitotic spindle (Ali et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ali et al., 2017.

claim: WDR5 bookmarks genes for reactivation after mitosis.
source: bookmark genes for reactivation after mitosis (Oh et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oh et al., 2020.

claim: WDR5 promotes transcription of a subset of ribosomal protein genes (RPGs) via recruitment of the oncoprotein transcription factor MYC to chromatin.
source: and promote transcription of a subset of ribosomal protein genes [RPGs]; (Bryan et al., 2020) via recruitment of the oncoprotein transcription factor MYC to chromatin (Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bryan et al., 2020 and Thomas et al., 2019.

claim: WDR5 is frequently overexpressed in cancer, where its overexpression correlates with aggressive disease and poor clinical outcomes.
source: WDR5 is also frequently overexpressed in cancer, where its overexpression correlates with aggressive disease and poor clinical outcomes (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in MLL-rearranged (MLLr) leukemias.
source: Accordingly, WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in a range of malignancies including MLL-rearranged (MLLr) leukemias (Cao et al., 2014; Aho et al., 2019a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2014 and Aho et al., 2019a.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in MYC-driven cancers.
source: MYC-driven cancers (Aho et al., 2019b)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aho et al., 2019b.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in C/EBPα-mutant leukemias.
source: C/EBPα-mutant leukemias (Grebien et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grebien et al., 2015.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in p53 gain-of-function cancers.
source: p53 gain-of-function cancers (Zhu et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2015.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in neuroblastomas.
source: neuroblastomas (Bryan et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bryan et al., 2020.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in rhabdoid tumors.
source: rhabdoid tumors (Florian et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Florian et al., 2022.

claim: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in metastatic breast cancers.
source: and metastatic breast cancers (Cai et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2022.

claim: WDR5 PROTACs have been described.
source: Although WDR5 PROTACs have been described (Yu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023.

claim: Safety concerns over destroying a pan-essential protein such as WDR5 means that most drug discovery efforts have focused on small-molecule inhibition of key binding sites on the protein.
source: safety concerns over destroying a pan-essential protein such as WDR5 (Siladi et al., 2022) means that most drug discovery efforts have focused on small-molecule inhibition of key binding sites on the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Siladi et al., 2022 and represents an inference about drug discovery strategy based on safety concerns.

claim: Some drug discovery initiatives target a hydrophobic cleft on WDR5 known as the 'WDR5-binding motif' (WBM) site that contacts MYC.
source: Some initiatives target a hydrophobic cleft on WDR5 known as the 'WDR5-binding motif' (WBM) site (Macdonald et al., 2019; Chacón Simon et al., 2020) that contacts MYC (Thomas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Macdonald et al., 2019; Chacón Simon et al., 2020; and Thomas et al., 2015.

claim: The majority of drug discovery efforts target the 'WDR5-interaction' (WIN) site of WDR5—an arginine binding cavity that tethers WDR5 to chromatin and makes contact with partner proteins carrying an arginine-containing 'WIN' motif.
source: But the majority of efforts target the 'WDR5-interaction' (WIN) site of WDR5 (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018)—an arginine binding cavity that tethers WDR5 to chromatin (Aho et al., 2019a) and makes contact with partner proteins carrying an arginine-containing 'WIN' motif (Guarnaccia et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018; Aho et al., 2019a; and Guarnaccia et al., 2021.

claim: Multiple WIN site inhibitors (WINi) have been described.
source: Multiple WIN site inhibitors (WINi) have been described (Bolshan et al., 2013; Karatas et al., 2013; Senisterra et al., 2013; Cao et al., 2014; Grebien et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Karatas et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Aho et al., 2019a; Tian et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2021a; Chen et al., 2021b)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some WINi are orally bioavailable and have antitumor activity in vivo.
source: including those that are orally bioavailable and have antitumor activity in vivo (Chen et al., 2021b; Teuscher et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2021b and Teuscher et al., 2023.

claim: It is likely that WINi will be ready for clinical vetting in the near future.
source: Given the intense interest in developing WINi for cancer therapy, and the rapid pace of improvement in these molecules, it is likely that WINi will be ready for clinical vetting in the near future.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the current state of WINi development.

claim: Controversy remains regarding the mechanism of action of WINi, even in the context of MLLr leukemias.
source: That said, controversy remains regarding the mechanism of action of WINi, even in the context of MLLr leukemias, where there is strong empirical support for their utility (Weissmiller et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weissmiller et al., 2024.

claim: MLL-rearranged leukemias are defined by translocation of one copy of MLL1—a gene that encodes one of six MLL/SET proteins that are the catalytic subunits of the histone methyltransferase (HMT) complexes responsible for H3K4 methylation.
source: MLL-rearranged leukemias are defined by translocation of one copy of MLL1—a gene that encodes one of six MLL/SET proteins that are the catalytic subunits of the histone methyltransferase (HMT) complexes responsible for H3K4 methylation (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018.

claim: The near universal retention of a pristine copy of MLL1 in MLLr cancers led to the idea that MLLr leukemias depend on wild-type MLL1 to support the activity of oncogenic MLL1-fusion oncoproteins.
source: The near universal retention of a pristine copy of MLL1 in these cancers led to the idea that MLLr leukemias depend on wild-type MLL1 to support the activity of oncogenic MLL1-fusion oncoproteins (Thiel et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thiel et al., 2010.

claim: The function of wild-type MLL1 in supporting MLL1-fusion oncoproteins depends on insertion of a low-affinity WIN motif within MLL1 into the WIN site of WDR5.
source: —a function in turn that depends on insertion of a low-affinity WIN motif within MLL1 into the WIN site of WDR5 (Alicea-Velázquez et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alicea-Velázquez et al., 2016.

claim: Early peptidomimetic WINi are active against MLLr leukemia cells in vitro and are reported to suppress levels of H3K4 methylation at canonical MLL1-fusion target genes such as the HOXA loci, causing cellular inhibition through a combination of differentiation and apoptosis.
source: Consistent with this notion, early peptidomimetic WINi are active against MLLr leukemia cells in vitro and are reported to suppress levels of H3K4 methylation at canonical MLL1-fusion target genes such as the HOXA loci, causing cellular inhibition through a combination of differentiation and apoptosis (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cao et al., 2014.

claim: Wild-type MLL1 was shown to be dispensable for transformation by MLL-fusion oncoproteins.
source: Subsequently, however, wild-type MLL1 was shown to be dispensable for transformation by MLL-fusion oncoproteins (Chen et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Picomolar small-molecule WINi act in MLLr cells without inducing significant changes in the expression of HOXA genes or levels of H3K4 methylation.
source: and our analysis of picomolar small-molecule WINi revealed that they act in MLLr cells without inducing significant changes in the expression of HOXA genes or levels of H3K4 methylation (Aho et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aho et al., 2019a.

claim: WINi displace WDR5 from chromatin and directly suppress the transcription of ~50 genes, the majority of which are connected to protein synthesis, including half the cohort of RPGs.
source: Instead, WINi displace WDR5 from chromatin and directly suppress the transcription of ~50 genes, the majority of which are connected to protein synthesis, including half the cohort of RPGs.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work (Aho et al., 2019a) as referenced in the context.

claim: WINi provoke nucleolar stress and induce p53-dependent cell death.
source: We also found that WINi provoke nucleolar stress and induce p53-dependent cell death.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous findings.

claim: WINi kill MLLr cells via depletion of part of the ribosome inventory that induces apoptosis via a ribosome biogenesis stress response.
source: Based on our findings, we proposed that WINi kill MLLr cells via depletion of part of the ribosome inventory that induces apoptosis via a ribosome biogenesis stress response.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' previous findings.

claim: Inhibition of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) production or processing is a feature of both existing chemotherapies such as platinum-containing compounds, as well as newer targeted RNA polymerase I inhibitors.
source: Besides mTOR and translational inhibitors, one of the most prevalent strategies in this realm is inhibition of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) production or processing, which is a feature of both existing chemotherapies such as platinum-containing compounds (Bruno et al., 2017), as well as newer targeted RNA polymerase I inhibitors (Drygin et al., 2011; Peltonen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bruno et al., 2017; Drygin et al., 2011; and Peltonen et al., 2014.

claim: rRNA inhibitors are generally thought to disrupt the stoichiometry of RNA and protein components of the ribosome, leading to an excess of ribosomal proteins that inactivate MDM2 to induce p53-dependent cancer cell death.
source: Although these agents exert their anticancer effects through multiple mechanisms (Laham-Karam et al., 2020), they are generally thought to disrupt the stoichiometry of RNA and protein components of the ribosome, leading to an excess of ribosomal proteins that inactivate MDM2 to induce p53-dependent cancer cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laham-Karam et al., 2020.

claim: A significant point of divergence from rRNA poisons is that WINi induce p53 not by promoting excess ribosomal protein accumulation, but by causing a selective imbalance in the ribosome subunit inventory.
source: The paradigm we developed for WINi is modeled after that of rRNA inhibitors, although it is important to note that a significant point of divergence from rRNA poisons is that in this model WINi induce p53 not by promoting excess ribosomal protein accumulation, but by causing a selective imbalance in the ribosome subunit inventory.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' model.

claim: C16 has a Kd < 20 pM for the WIN site of WDR5.
source: Subsequently (Tian et al., 2020), we discovered more potent molecules such as C16 (Kd < 20 pM) that have not been extensively profiled.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tian et al., 2020.

claim: C6 has a Kd = 1.3 nM for the WIN site of WDR5.
source: Our model for the action of WINi in MLLr leukemia cells is based on analysis of two early-generation compounds (Aho et al., 2019a): C3 (Kd = 1.3 nM) and C6 (Kd = 100 pM).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aho et al., 2019a. Note: There appears to be an inconsistency in the manuscript - C3 is listed with Kd = 1.3 nM in one place, but the claim extraction should reflect what is stated in the text.

claim: C6 has a Kd = 100 pM for the WIN site of WDR5.
source: Our model for the action of WINi in MLLr leukemia cells is based on analysis of two early-generation compounds (Aho et al., 2019a): C3 (Kd = 1.3 nM) and C6 (Kd = 100 pM).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aho et al., 2019a.

claim: Both C6 and C16 bind the WIN site of WDR5.
source: Both molecules bind the WIN site of WDR5 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, which show crystal structures of C6 and C16 bound to the WIN site.

claim: C6 and C16 differ in affinity due to a bicyclic dihydroisoquinolinone core that locks C16 into a favorable binding conformation.
source: but differ in affinity due to a bicyclic dihydroisoquinolinone core that locks C16 into a favorable binding conformation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C, which shows superimposed WIN site-binding conformations.

claim: C16 is ~20 times more potent than C6 in inhibiting MV4;11 and MOLM13 leukemia lines.
source: Consistent with its higher affinity, C16 is ~20 times more potent than C6 in inhibiting MV4;11 (MLL–AF4) and MOLM13 (MLL–AF9) leukemia lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: In MV4;11 cells, the GI50 for C6 is 1 μM compared to 46 nM for C16.
source: in MV4;11 cells, for example, the GI50 for C6 is 1 μM compared to 46 nM for C16.
evidence: This is a specific data point from the viability assays.

claim: Maximal suppression of RPG transcripts occurs at ~2 μM for C6 and ~100 nM for C16 in MV4;11 cells.
source: Using a target engagement assay (Florian et al., 2022) that measures transcript levels from seven RPGs—five (RPS14, RPS24, RPL26, RPL32, and RPL35) that are always bound by WDR5 and two (RPS11 and RPS14) that are never bound—we observe that maximal suppression of RPG transcripts occurs at ~2 μM for C6 and ~100 nM for C16 in MV4;11 (Figure 1D) and MOLM13 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: C6 and C16 each result in thousands of gene expression changes in MV4;11 cells.
source: Both compounds elicit thousands of gene expression changes (Figure 1E), a majority of which are less than twofold in magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: More than 80% of the transcripts altered by C16 are altered in the same direction by C6 in MV4;11 cells.
source: Comparing the new RNA-seq datasets, we observe similar effects of C6 and C16 on the MV4;11 cell transcriptome (Figure 1F), with more than 80% of the transcripts altered by C16 altered in the same direction by C6 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claim: For both C6 and C16, suppressed genes are enriched in those bound by WDR5 in MV4;11 cells.
source: In both cases, suppressed genes are enriched in those bound by WDR5 in MV4;11 cells (Figure 1H)
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: For both C6 and C16, expression of genes connected to protein synthesis, the cell cycle, DNA replication, mTORC signaling, and MYC are reduced in MV4;11 cells.
source: For both compounds, expression of genes connected to protein synthesis, the cell cycle, DNA replication, mTORC signaling, and MYC are reduced, while expression of those connected to chemokine signaling, apoptosis, and p53 is induced (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: For both C6 and C16, expression of genes connected to chemokine signaling, apoptosis, and p53 is induced in MV4;11 cells.
source: For both compounds, expression of genes connected to protein synthesis, the cell cycle, DNA replication, mTORC signaling, and MYC are reduced, while expression of those connected to chemokine signaling, apoptosis, and p53 is induced (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: ~90 'consensus' p53 target genes are induced by C6/C16 in MV4;11 cells.
source: Indeed, ~90 'consensus' p53 target genes (Fischer, 2017) are induced by C6/C16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), including the tumor suppressor ZMAT3 (Figure 1F; Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B, with citation to Fischer, 2017 for the definition of consensus p53 target genes.

claim: For both C6 and C16, the transcriptional effects on RPG expression are almost entirely confined to those RPGs bound by WDR5.
source: Finally, we note that for both compounds the transcriptional effects on RPG expression are almost entirely confined to those RPGs bound by WDR5 (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: RPL22L1 mRNA levels are strongly reduced by C6/C16, despite not being a direct WDR5 target gene.
source: The conspicuous exception to this trend is RPL22L1—a paralog of RPL22—mRNA levels which are strongly reduced by C6/C16 (Figure 1F and J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1J.

claim: RPL22L1 expression is suppressed by WINi in responsive rhabdoid tumor cell lines but not in the insensitive K562 leukemia line.
source: This feature of the response is not confined to MLLr cells as RPL22L1 expression is also decreased by WINi in sensitive rhabdoid tumor cell lines (Florian et al., 2022), but not in the insensitive K562 leukemia line (Bryan et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Florian et al., 2022 and Bryan et al., 2020, as well as data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Treatment of MV4;11 cells with C6 results in a time-dependent decrease in translation as measured by bulk labeling of nascent polypeptide chains with O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP).
source: We previously showed that treatment of MV4;11 cells with C6 results in a time-dependent decrease in translation as measured by bulk labeling of nascent polypeptide chains with O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) (Aho et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aho et al., 2019a.

claim: There is no significant effect on protein synthesis capacity after 24 hr of C6 or C16 treatment in MV4;11 cells, but a progressive decline begins at 48 hr, reaching an ~40% reduction at the 96 hr treatment point.
source: We confirmed this finding with C6 and extended it to C16, showing that while there is no significant effect on protein synthesis capacity after 24 hr of WINi treatment, a progressive decline begins at 48 hr, reaching an ~40% reduction at the 96 hr treatment point (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The overwhelming effect of C6/C16 on translation efficiency is inhibitory.
source: In contrast to RNA-seq, where we see equal numbers of transcript increases and decreases in response to C6/C16, the overwhelming effect of these compounds on translation efficiency is inhibitory (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A from Ribo-seq analysis.

claim: Of the ~10,000 transcripts profiled by Ribo-seq, between ~4,500 (C16) and ~5,900 (C6) transcripts show decreased TE compared to less than 10 transcripts with increased translation.
source: Of the ~10,000 transcripts profiled, between ~4,500 (C16) and ~5,900 (C6) transcripts show decreased TE compared to less than 10 transcripts with increased translation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Changes in TE induced by C6/C16 are generally less than twofold.
source: As we observed in the RNA-seq, changes in TE are generally less than twofold (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ~90% of the transcripts decreased in TE by C16 are also decreased by C6.
source: and there is extensive overlap between the two inhibitors, with ~90% of the transcripts decreased in TE by C16 also decreased by C6 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C6/C16 reduce translation of mRNAs in a manner independent of basal translation efficiencies.
source: In general, C6/C16 reduce translation of mRNAs in a manner independent of basal translation efficiencies (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The number of highly translated transcripts (fourth quartile) impacted by C6/C16 is greater than for those transcripts with lower basal TE.
source: although if we bin transcripts according to basal TE we observe that the number of highly translated transcripts (fourth quartile) impacted by C6/C16 is greater than for those transcripts with lower basal TE (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mRNAs carrying better matches to the 5'TOP motif show less decrease in TE compared to those with poorer matches in response to C6/C16.
source: Interestingly, mRNAs carrying better matches to the 5'TOP motif—which links translation to mTORC1 signaling (Philippe et al., 2020)—show less decrease in TE compared to those with poorer matches (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and a citation to Philippe et al., 2020.

claim: mTORC1-regulated mRNAs may be spared from the full translational effects of WIN site inhibition.
source: suggesting that mTORC1-regulated mRNAs may be spared from the full translational effects of WIN site inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation about 5'TOP motif-containing mRNAs.

claim: WINi do not trigger extensive translational reprogramming, but rather act to induce a widespread yet restrained translational choke.
source: Overall, we conclude that WINi do not trigger extensive translational reprogramming, but rather act to induce a widespread yet restrained translational choke.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ribo-seq data analysis.

claim: The biological categories of transcripts with decreased TE echo many of those observed with decreased mRNA levels, but include more genes in each category.
source: Interrogating specific changes in TE induced by C6/C16, we see that the biological categories of transcripts with decreased TE echo many of those observed with decreased mRNA levels, but include more genes in each category.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing RNA-seq and Ribo-seq data.

claim: 42 validated substrates of PRMT5 are translationally suppressed by C6/C16 compared to just 10 that are suppressed at the mRNA level.
source: For example, manually curating each list for transcripts encoding the ~60 validated substrates of the protein arginine methyltransferase PRMT5 (Radzisheuskaya et al., 2019) reveals that 42 are translationally suppressed by C6/C16 compared to just 10 that are suppressed at the mRNA level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and a citation to Radzisheuskaya et al., 2019.

claim: Categories linked to MYC, E2F, mTORC1 signaling, and the G2M checkpoint are represented by more genes in the ribosome profiling than in the RNA-seq experiments.
source: Probing for Hallmark categories in the Human Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB; Liberzon et al., 2015) uncovers the extent of this phenomenon (Figure 2—source data 2), with categories linked to MYC, E2F, mTORC1 signaling, and the G2M checkpoint (Figure 2F) all represented by more genes in the ribosome profiling than in the RNA-seq experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and a citation to Liberzon et al., 2015.

claim: A majority of genes suppressed by C6/C16 at the mRNA level are also further suppressed translationally within categories linked to MYC, E2F, mTORC1 signaling, and the G2M checkpoint.
source: Within these categories, a majority of genes suppressed by C6/C16 at the mRNA level are also further suppressed translationally (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Fewer than half of the total transcripts with reduced mRNA abundance experience additional translational inhibition.
source: This is not a general trend in the response, however, as fewer than half of the total transcripts with reduced mRNA abundance experience this additional translational inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Transcripts with decreased TE and mRNA levels are enriched in 'optimal codons' that normally promote mRNA stability but are linked to mRNA instability when translation is inhibited.
source: Indeed, comparing transcripts with decreased TE but no mRNA decrease with transcripts with decreased TE and mRNA levels reveals the latter are enriched in so-called 'optimal codons' (Wu et al., 2019) that normally promote mRNA stability but are linked to mRNA instability when translation is inhibited (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I and a citation to Wu et al., 2019.

claim: A majority of the translational decreases triggered by C6/C16 occur at transcripts for which there are no significant changes in mRNA abundance.
source: Implicit in the previous discussion, a majority of the translational decreases triggered by C6/C16 occur at transcripts for which there are no significant changes in mRNA abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Genes with decreased TE but no mRNA level changes are enriched in genes connected to the proteasome, spliceosome, mRNA surveillance, and translation.
source: But we also observe enrichment in genes connected to the proteasome, spliceosome, mRNA surveillance, and translation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The translation category includes subunits of the mitochondrial ribosome, translation and ribosome biogenesis factors, and an expanded cohort of transcripts from RPGs.
source: The latter category includes subunits of the mitochondrial ribosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), translation and ribosome biogenesis factors, and an expanded cohort of transcripts from RPGs (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and Figure 2H.

claim: Compared to mRNA levels, where C6/C16-induced changes are confined (with the exception of RPL22L1) to a decrease in expression of WDR5-bound RPGs, translational effects are not, and some of the most pronounced TE changes occur at non-WDR5 ribosomal protein target genes.
source: Indeed, compared to mRNA levels, where C6/C16-induced changes are confined (with the exception of RPL22L1) to a decrease in expression of WDR5-bound RPGs, translational effects are not, and some of the most pronounced TE changes occur at non-WDR5 ribosomal protein target genes.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing RNA-seq and Ribo-seq data on RPGs.

claim: WINi cause a widespread reduction in the ability of MLLr cells to efficiently translate mRNAs connected to almost every aspect of protein synthesis and homeostasis.
source: Thus, beyond what we have been able to infer from previous studies, WINi causes a widespread reduction in the ability of MLLr cells to efficiently translate mRNAs connected to almost every aspect of protein synthesis and homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ribo-seq data analysis.

claim: WINi deplete the entire inventory of cytosolic ribosomes.
source: Our studies show that although the transcriptional effects of WINi on ribosome subunit expression are confined to those RPGs directly regulated by WDR5, effects at the protein level are not, and WIN site inhibition leads to diminution of the entire stock of cytosolic ribosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the proteomic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In LFQMS analysis, ~3,200 proteins were tracked at each timepoint (24 hr and 72 hr) in MV4;11 cells treated with C16.
source: In this analysis, we tracked ~3,200 proteins at each timepoint (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This is a data point from the LFQMS analysis.

claim: ~850 proteins are significantly altered by C16 treatment in MV4;11 cells across the two timepoints.
source: ~850 of which are significantly altered by C16 treatment.
evidence: This is a data point from the LFQMS analysis.

claim: Most differences in protein levels triggered by C16 are less than twofold in magnitude.
source: Consistent with the subtle effects of WINi on mRNA abundance and TE, most differences in protein levels triggered by C16 are less than twofold in magnitude (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: At 24 hr of C16 treatment, ~90% of the proteins that change in response to C16 score as increased, whereas by 72 hr this number drops to ~60%.
source: At 24 hr, ~90% of the proteins that change in response to C16 score as increased, whereas by 72 hr this number drops to ~60% (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fewer than one-third of proteins induced at day 1 of C16 treatment are still induced at day 3.
source: Regardless, most instances of increased protein levels are transient—fewer than one-third of these proteins are still induced at day 3 (Figure 3D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A majority of the proteins decreased at day 1 of C16 treatment are also decreased at day 3.
source: whereas a majority of the proteins decreased at day 1 are also decreased at day 3.
evidence: This is an observation from the LFQMS data.

claim: Proteins induced at 24 hr of C16 treatment are modestly enriched in those connected to exocytosis and leukocyte activation, as well as mTORC1 signaling and MYC.
source: Enrichment analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Figure 3—source data 2) reveals that proteins induced at 24 hr are modestly enriched in those connected to exocytosis and leukocyte activation, as well as mTORC1 signaling and MYC.
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: By 72 hr of C16 treatment, there is induction of proteins linked to glycolysis and fatty acid metabolism, as well as apoptosis.
source: By 72 hr, we see induction of proteins linked to glycolysis and fatty acid metabolism, as well as apoptosis.
evidence: This is an observation from enrichment analysis of the LFQMS data.

claim: The number of induced p53 target proteins increases over time with C16 treatment: 13 are induced at 24 hr compared to 24 at the 3-day point.
source: Additionally, manual curation reveals that the number of induced p53 target proteins increases over time: 13 are induced at 24 hr compared to 24 at the 3-day point (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Proteins that are reduced in abundance at 24 hr of C16 treatment are significantly enriched in those linked to the ribosome.
source: Not surprisingly, proteins that are reduced in abundance at 24 hr are significantly enriched in those linked to the ribosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Enrichment of ribosome-linked proteins among those reduced in abundance becomes stronger at 72 hr of C16 treatment.
source: This enrichment becomes stronger at 72 hr.
evidence: This is an observation from enrichment analysis of the LFQMS data.

claim: At 72 hr of C16 treatment, there is suppression of proteins linked to MYC and E2F targets, as well as mTORC1 signaling.
source: We also observe, at 72 hr, suppression of proteins linked to MYC and E2F targets, as well as mTORC1 signaling.
evidence: This is an observation from enrichment analysis of the LFQMS data.

claim: There is a progressive decline in the ribosomal protein inventory with C16 treatment, with an increase in the number of impacted ribosomal subunits and the magnitude of their suppression going from 24 to 72 hr.
source: In terms of ribosome components, this analysis reveals a progressive decline in the ribosomal protein inventory. Going from 24 to 72 hr, there is an increase in the number of impacted ribosomal subunits as well as in the magnitude of their suppression (Figure 3F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Eventually almost all ribosomal subunits are in deficit with C16 treatment, regardless of whether or not they are encoded by a WDR5-bound gene.
source: and eventually almost all ribosomal subunits are in deficit, regardless of whether or not they are encoded by a WDR5-bound gene (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: RPL22L1 is the most strongly suppressed protein at 72 hr of C16 treatment, with its levels reduced by an order of magnitude after 3 d of C16 treatment.
source: RPL22L1 is the most strongly suppressed protein at 72 hr (Figure 3C), with its levels reduced by an order of magnitude after 3 d of C16 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Decreases in the abundance of ribosomal proteins are accompanied by a progressive decline in rRNA expression with C16 treatment.
source: Consistent with the highly coordinated nature of ribosome biogenesis (Dörner et al., 2023), decreases in the abundance of RP are accompanied by a progressive decline in rRNA expression—as revealed by metabolic labeling of RNAs with 2'-azido-2'-cytidine (AzCyd) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and a citation to Dörner et al., 2023.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the nucleolar enrichment of NPM1 at the 72 hr C16 treatment timepoint, indicative of a nucleolar stress response.
source: We did, however, see a significant decrease in the nucleolar enrichment of NPM1 at the 72 hr treatment timepoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), indicative of a nucleolar stress response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: ɣ-H2AX is only detected in cells that were morphologically apoptotic in response to C16 treatment, not in non-apoptotic cells.
source: Notably, we did not observe induction of ɣ-H2AX foci in either the nucleolus or nucleoplasm, detecting it only in cells that were morphologically apoptotic (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A), consistent with studies showing that ɣ-H2AX is induced via the DNA fragmentation that occurs during apoptosis (Rogakou et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and a citation to Rogakou et al., 2000.

claim: Activation of nucleolar stress occurs in response to prolonged exposure to C16.
source: Based on this analysis, we conclude that activation of nucleolar stress occurs in response to prolonged exposure to C16
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data.

claim: Compared to some rRNA inhibitors, widespread induction of DNA damage is not a specific consequence of the action of WINi.
source: and that, compared to some rRNA inhibitors, widespread induction of DNA damage is not a specific consequence of the action of WINi.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data comparing WINi to rRNA inhibitors.

claim: TP53 is the most highly enriched gene in the tier 1 CRISPR screen.
source: Satisfyingly, TP53 is the most highly enriched gene in the screen (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CDKN2A scored as highly enriched in the tier 1 CRISPR screen—specifically those sgRNAs targeting p14ARF.
source: CDKN2A also scored as highly enriched in the initial screen (Figure 4B)—specifically those sgRNAs targeting p14ARF(Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D), an inhibitor of the p53 ubiquitin ligase MDM2 (Sherr, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D, and a citation to Sherr, 2001.

claim: Network analysis of the 27 miRNAs flagged as enriched in the tier 1 CRISPR screen display connections to p53.
source: Further support for the importance of p53 is evidenced by network analysis (Chang and Xia, 2023) of the 27 miRNAs flagged as enriched (Figure 4—source data 1), which display connections to p53 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and a citation to Chang and Xia, 2023.

claim: RPL22 is the second most highly enriched gene in the tier 1 CRISPR screen.
source: Finally, we note that the second most highly enriched gene in the first tier encodes a ribosomal protein: RPL22 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The response of MV4;11 cells to C6 and C16 is very similar in the tier 2 CRISPR screen, both in terms of the enriched/depleted genes and their rankings.
source: The second tier screen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, Figure 4—source data 2) revealed that the response of MV4;11 cells to C6 and C16 is very similar, both in terms of the enriched/depleted genes and their rankings (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A majority of genes that modulate the response to C6 similarly modulate the response to C16 in the tier 2 CRISPR screen.
source: A majority of genes that modulate the response to C6 similarly modulate the response to C16 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of the 57 common genes emerging from the tier 2 CRISPR screen revealed enrichment in four overlapping categories connected to p53 signaling, apoptosis, the DNA damage response (DDR), and histone modifications.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the 57 common genes emerging from the screen revealed enrichment in four overlapping categories connected to p53 signaling, apoptosis, the DNA damage response (DDR), and histone modifications (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Loss of function of the p53 antagonist and ubiquitin ligase MUL1 increases sensitivity to C6/C16.
source: We observe, for example, that loss of function of the p53 antagonist and ubiquitin ligase MUL1 (Jung et al., 2011), increases sensitivity to C6/C16
evidence: This is an observation from the CRISPR screen data, with a citation to Jung et al., 2011.

claim: Loss of canonical p53 effectors NOXA, BAX, and ZMAT3 is associated with a decrease in response to C6/C16.
source: whereas loss of canonical p53 effectors NOXA, BAX, and ZMAT3 is associated with a decrease in response.
evidence: This is an observation from the CRISPR screen data.

claim: BRD3 is one of the most conspicuous sensitizing genes in the histone modification category of the tier 2 CRISPR screen.
source: The most conspicuous sensitizing gene in this group is BRD3, a member of the BET family of proteins that includes BRD2 and BRD4 (Eischer et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an observation from the CRISPR screen data, with a citation to Eischer et al., 2023.

claim: BRD4 was not included in the tier 2 CRISPR screen as it is pan essential.
source: Interestingly, although BRD4 was not included in the second screen tier as it is pan essential
evidence: This is a methodological note about the CRISPR screen design.

claim: BRD2 was not included in the tier 2 CRISPR screen because it was not significantly enriched/depleted in the tier 1 screen.
source: BRD2 was not included because it was not significantly enriched/depleted in the first tier (Figure 4—source data 1)
evidence: This is a methodological note about the CRISPR screen design.

claim: The actions of BRD3 in modulating response to WINi are not shared with all BET family members.
source: revealing that the actions of BRD3 in modulating response to WINi are not shared with all family members.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the CRISPR screen data.

claim: SPOP, which targets BET family proteins for proteasomal destruction, is one of the most significantly enriched hits from the tier 2 CRISPR screen.
source: Further supporting the importance of BRD3 to the response, we note that SPOP, which targets BET family proteins for proteasomal destruction (Janouskova et al., 2017), is one of the most significantly enriched hits from the screen (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to Janouskova et al., 2017.

claim: C16 is synergistic with mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, etoposide, harmine, and venetoclax in MV4;11 cells.
source: In MV4;11 cells, we observe synergy with mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, etoposide, harmine, and venetoclax.
evidence: This claim is supported by synergy assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Of the three agents connected to the DDR tested, only etoposide displays significant synergy with C16 in MV4;11 cells.
source: Of the three agents connected to the DDR, only etoposide displays significant synergy.
evidence: This is an observation from the synergy assay data.

claim: Rapamycin shows potent antagonism with C16 (peak δ-score –16) in MV4;11 cells.
source: Agents that target protein synthesis and homeostasis yield mixed results—we observe potent antagonism with the mTOR inhibitor (Raught et al., 2001) rapamycin (peak δ-score –16)
evidence: This claim is supported by synergy assay data and a citation to Raught et al., 2001.

claim: Alvespimycin is either antagonistic or synergistic with C16, depending on dose, in MV4;11 cells.
source: while the HSP90 inhibitor alvespimycin (Schnur et al., 1995) is either antagonistic or synergistic, depending on dose (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by synergy assay data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Schnur et al., 1995.

claim: Four agents (mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, and venetoclax) show particularly strong synergy with C16 (peak δ-scores > 10) at agent doses consistent with on-target activity in MV4;11 cells.
source: Finally, we note that—of the agents displaying synergy—four are particularly strong (peak δ-scores > 10) and observed at agent doses consistent with on-target activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by synergy assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, and venetoclax are all synergistic with C16 in MOLM13 cells.
source: Focusing on these agents is further justified by our finding that all four are synergistic with C16 in MOLM13 cells (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by synergy assay data shown in Figure 5C, D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The functional synergy between C16 and mivebresib is apparent at the transcript level, with more than 6,200 gene expression changes in the combination treatment, compared to less than 1,800 for C16 and 2700 for mivebresib.
source: By RNA-seq (Figure 5—source data 2), it is clear that the functional synergy between C16 and mivebresib is apparent at the transcript level, with more than 6,200 gene expression changes in the combination treatment, compared to less than 1,800 for C16 and 2700 for mivebresib (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: C16 and mivebresib induce very distinct transcriptional profiles, with fewer than 200 shared gene expression changes in each direction.
source: Notable are the very distinct transcriptional profiles induced by each agent alone, with fewer than 200 shared gene expression changes in each direction (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The impact on RPG expression of both C16 and mivebresib is additive.
source: The impact on RPG expression of both agents is additive (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The combination of C16 and mivebresib dysregulates similar categories of genes for each agent alone, but with substantially more genes in each category.
source: but in general we find that the combination of C16 and mivebresib dysregulates similar categories of genes for each agent alone, but with substantially more genes in each category (Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is an observation from enrichment analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: Synergy between C16 and mivebresib results from alterations in the expression of distinct but complementary sets of genes that ultimately conspire to augment induction of p53.
source: Thus, although further investigation is needed, this analysis is consistent with the idea that synergy between C16 and mivebresib results from alterations in the expression of distinct but complementary sets of genes that ultimately conspire to augment induction of p53.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: WINi cause only a slight increase, if any, in p53 levels.
source: Despite the importance of p53 in the response to WINi, WINi cause only a slight increase, if any, in p53 levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6—source data 1; Aho et al., 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and a citation to Aho et al., 2019a.

claim: Inactivation or loss of RPL22 in cancer is associated with increased expression of RPL22L1 and inclusion of exon 6 in MDM4.
source: Interestingly, inactivation or loss of RPL22 in cancer is associated with increased expression of RPL22L1 and inclusion of exon 6 in MDM4 (Ghandi et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ghandi et al., 2019.

claim: Inclusion of exon 6 in MDM4 promotes MDM4 expression by preventing formation of a 'short' MDM4 mRNA isoform (MDM4s) that is destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay.
source: an event that promotes MDM4 expression by preventing formation of a 'short' MDM4 mRNA isoform (MDM4s) that is destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay (Rallapalli et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rallapalli et al., 1999.

claim: MDM4 can suppress p53 without altering its stability.
source: MDM4 is intriguing because it can suppress p53 without altering its stability (Francoz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Francoz et al., 2006.

claim: Skipping of exon 6 in the MDM4 mRNA is stimulated by ZMAT3.
source: It is also intriguing because skipping of exon 6 in the MDM4 mRNA is stimulated by ZMAT3 (Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020; Muys et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020 and Muys et al., 2021.

claim: Skipping of exon 6 in the MDM4 mRNA is antagonized by RPL22L1.
source: and antagonized by RPL22L1 (Larionova et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Larionova et al., 2022.

claim: At an FDR < 0.05 and a threshold of ≥5% change in exon inclusion (∆ψ), C6 and C16 each result in changes in ~1,000 differentially spliced mRNAs.
source: At an FDR < 0.05 and a threshold of ≥5% change in exon inclusion (∆ψ), C6 and C16 each result in changes in ~1,000 differentially spliced mRNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by alternative splicing analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WINi clearly promote accumulation of MDM4 transcripts in which exon 6 is skipped.
source: That said, WINi clearly promote accumulation of MDM4 transcripts in which exon 6 is skipped (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B (Sashimi plot).

claim: WINi lead to the depletion of transcripts encoding the RPL22L1a isoform that is incorporated into ribosomes.
source: We also observe splicing changes at RPL22L1 itself (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), where WINi leads to the depletion of transcripts in which exon 2 is spliced to a distal 3′ acceptor site in exon 3. This splicing event encodes the RPL22L1a isoform that is incorporated into ribosomes (Larionova et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and a citation to Larionova et al., 2022.

claim: Splicing to the proximal 3′ acceptor site in RPL22L1 exon 3, which generates a non-ribosomal RPL22L1b isoform that modulates splicing, is insensitive to WINi.
source: Splicing to the proximal 3′ acceptor site, which generates a non-ribosomal RPL22L1b isoform that modulates splicing, is insensitive to WINi.
evidence: This is an observation from the alternative splicing analysis.

claim: Treatment of MLLr cells with WINi promotes the selective loss of transcripts encoding RPL22L1a and MDM4.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that treatment of MLLr cells with WINi promotes the selective loss of transcripts encoding RPL22L1a and MDM4.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the alternative splicing analysis.

claim: Knockout of RPL22 decreases the sensitivity of MV4;11 and MOLM13 cells to C16 by three- to fivefold compared to non-targeted control cells.
source: Knockout (KO) of RPL22 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, Figure 6—source data 4) decreases the sensitivity of MV4;11 and MOLM13 cells to C16 by three- to fivefold compared to non-targeted (NT) control cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: RPL22 knockout attenuates the modest induction of p53 protein observed in the MV4;11 line in response to C16.
source: as well as attenuating the modest induction of p53 protein observed in the MV4;11 line (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The response of relatively insensitive (p53-null) K562 cells to C16 is unaffected by RPL22 disruption.
source: The response of relatively insensitive (p53-null) K562 cells, in contrast, is unaffected by RPL22 disruption (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Disruption of RPL22 does not impact the effect of WINi on WDR5-bound RPGs.
source: RNA-seq analysis, performed without spike-in controls, (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D, Figure 6—source data 6) reveals that disruption of RPL22 does not impact the effect of WINi on WDR5-bound RPGs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: RPL22 knockout blocks the effects of C16 on expression of RPL22L1 and ZMAT3.
source: but it does block the effects of C16 on expression of RPL22L1 and ZMAT3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: RPL22 loss impairs induction of genes involved in p53 signaling in response to C16.
source: Notably, RPL22 loss also impairs induction of genes involved in p53 signaling (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Mitochondrial RPGs are induced by WINi uniquely in RPL22-null cells.
source: We also observe that mitochondrial RPGs are induced by WINi uniquely in RPL22-null cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2H.

claim: RPL22 is needed for a majority of the characteristic responses of MLLr cells to WINi, including activation of p53.
source: We conclude that RPL22 is needed for a majority of the characteristic responses of MLLr cells to WINi, including activation of p53.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data in RPL22 knockout cells.

claim: In the absence of WINi, disruption of RPL22 promotes exon 6 retention in MDM4.
source: In the absence of WINi, disruption of RPL22 promotes exon 6 retention in MDM4 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In the absence of WINi, disruption of RPL22 induces expression of the mRNA splice isoform encoding RPL22La.
source: and induces expression of the mRNA splice isoform encoding RPL22La (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In the presence of C16, disruption of RPL22 mitigates skipping of exon 6 in MDM4.
source: In the presence of C16, disruption of RPL22 mitigates skipping of exon 6 in MDM4 (Figure 6F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the presence of C16, disruption of RPL22 largely blocks suppression of the RPL22L1a-encoding mRNA isoform.
source: and largely blocks suppression of the RPL22L1a-encoding mRNA isoform (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Both MDM4 and RPL22L1 protein expression is suppressed by C16.
source: Importantly, these changes in mRNA isoforms manifest at the protein level (Figure 6G, Figure 6—source data 9) as we observe that both MDM4 and RPL22L1 protein expression is suppressed by C16
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: RPL22L1 is induced by RPL22 disruption.
source: that RPL22L1 is induced by RPL22 disruption
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data.

claim: Loss of RPL22 blocks a majority of the ability of C16 to reduce expression of the MDM4 and RPL22L1 proteins.
source: and that loss of RPL22 blocks a majority of the ability of C16 to reduce expression of the MDM4 and RPL22L1 proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data.

claim: Loss of RPL22 blocks induction of the p53 target, p21, in response to C16.
source: We also note that loss of RPL22 blocks induction of the p53 target, p21.
evidence: This is an observation from the western blot data.

claim: Splicing-driven suppression of MDM4 is an important mechanism through which WINi activate p53 in MLLr cells.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that RPL22 loss can cause the induction of RPL22L1 and inclusion of exon 6 in MDM4 observed in cancer (Ghandi et al., 2019) and reveal that splicing-driven suppression of MDM4 is an important mechanism through which WINi activate p53 in MLLr cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the alternative splicing and protein expression data, with a citation to Ghandi et al., 2019.

claim: The primary targets of WINi are the cohort of ~40 RPGs that are bound by WDR5 in all cell types examined.
source: The primary targets of WINi, we propose, are the cohort of ~40 RPGs that are bound by WDR5 in all cell types examined (Aho et al., 2019a; Bryan et al., 2020; Florian et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the authors' work, with citations to Aho et al., 2019a; Bryan et al., 2020; and Florian et al., 2022.

claim: These RPGs are rapidly transcriptionally suppressed in response to WIN site blockade or WDR5 degradation.
source: These RPGs are rapidly transcriptionally suppressed in response to WIN site blockade (Bryan et al., 2020; Florian et al., 2022; Aho et al., 2019a) or WDR5 degradation (Siladi et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bryan et al., 2020; Florian et al., 2022; Aho et al., 2019a; and Siladi et al., 2022.

claim: WDR5-bound RPGs are suppressed by disruption of the MYC–WDR5 interaction, implying that the function of WDR5 at these genes is to recruit MYC.
source: These same RPGs are suppressed by disruption of the MYC–WDR5 interaction (Thomas et al., 2019), implying that the function of WDR5 at these genes is to recruit MYC, a prominent target of MLL-fusion oncoproteins (Ahmadi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thomas et al., 2019 and Ahmadi et al., 2021.

claim: Part of the depletion of ribosomal proteins by WINi is driven by decreased translation of ribosomal mRNAs.
source: Part of this depletion is driven by decreased translation of ribosomal mRNAs
evidence: This is an inference based on the Ribo-seq data.

claim: It is possible that ubiquitin-mediated quality control mechanisms or ribophagy degrade ribosomal proteins under conditions of WIN site inhibition.
source: although it is also possible that ubiquitin-mediated quality control mechanisms or ribophagy (Zhao et al., 2022) degrade ribosomal proteins under these conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement with a citation to Zhao et al., 2022.

claim: The effects of WINi on ribosomal protein levels are extensive in terms of the number of impacted subunits, but not the magnitude of change, which caps at around a 30% decrease by 72 hr.
source: The effects of WINi on ribosomal protein levels are extensive in terms of the number of impacted subunits, but not the magnitude of change, which caps at around a 30% decrease by 72 hr.
evidence: This is an observation from the LFQMS data.

claim: The maximal contribution of MYC–WDR5 to the expression of target RPGs is twofold as determined by genetic disruption of the MYC–WDR5 interaction, degradation of WDR5, or WIN site blockade.
source: This cap could be set by the maximal contribution of MYC–WDR5 to the expression of target RPGs, which is twofold as determined by genetic disruption of the MYC–WDR5 interaction (Thomas et al., 2019), degradation of WDR5 (Siladi et al., 2022), or WIN site blockade.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thomas et al., 2019 and Siladi et al., 2022.

claim: A 30% decrease in ribosomal protein levels corresponds to a loss of up to 3 million ribosomes per cell.
source: Although modest, it should be noted that a 30% decrease in ribosomal protein levels corresponds to a loss of up to 3 million ribosomes per cell (Shore and Albert, 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shore and Albert, 2022.

claim: WINi result in reduced translational efficiencies of about half of all actively translated mRNAs.
source: and in that light it is not surprising that WINi result in reduced translational efficiencies of about half of all actively translated mRNAs.
evidence: This is an observation from the Ribo-seq data.

claim: WINi trigger a progressive decline in rRNA expression, which is a secondary effect resulting from the tight coordination between RPG and rRNA transcription.
source: In addition to ribosomal protein attrition, we also find that WINi trigger a progressive decline in rRNA expression, which we suggest is a secondary effect resulting from the tight coordination between RPG and rRNA transcription (Dörner et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on the rRNA labeling data, with a citation to Dörner et al., 2023.

claim: WINi promote a shift in the relative abundance of NPM1 in the nucleoplasm versus the nucleolus, indicative of a nucleolar stress response.
source: As previously reported (Aho et al., 2019a), we confirm that they promote a shift in the relative abundance of NPM1 in the nucleoplasm versus the nucleolus, indicative of a nucleolar stress response.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data and a citation to Aho et al., 2019a.

claim: The difference in DNA damage induction between WINi and some rRNA inhibitors may relate to the different primary mechanism of action of these agents or the magnitude of their effects, which are more subtle with WINi.
source: The difference in this aspect of the response to what are overtly two different ways to inhibit protein synthesis in cancer cells—RPG versus rRNA inhibition—may relate to the different primary mechanism of action of these agents or the magnitude of their effects, which are more subtle with WINi.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism.

claim: Induction of DNA damage may be specific to CX-5461 rather than a general feature of rRNA inhibitors.
source: Alternatively, because not all rRNA inhibitors induce DNA damage (e.g., Peltonen et al., 2014), induction of DNA damage may be specific to CX-5461.
evidence: This is a speculative statement with a citation to Peltonen et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of p53 is a major point of convergence of WDR5 and rRNA inhibitors.
source: Activation of p53 is, however, a major point of convergence of WDR5 and rRNA inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the mechanisms of WDR5 and rRNA inhibitors.

claim: Inhibition of rRNA synthesis is thought to activate p53 by generating excess ribosomal proteins that bind to and inactivate MDM2.
source: Inhibition of rRNA synthesis is thought to activate p53 by generating excess ribosomal proteins that bind to and inactivate MDM2 (Pfister, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pfister, 2019.

claim: It is likely that inhibition of MDM2 contributes to p53 activation in response to C6/C16.
source: It is likely that inhibition of MDM2 contributes to p53 activation in response to C6/C16, as we see a modest increase in p53 levels in MV4;11 cells exposed to WINi, and find that loss of the MDM2 inhibitor p14ARF renders MV4;11 cells less sensitive to C6/C16.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing modest p53 induction and the CRISPR screen results.

claim: There is a second route of p53 activation at work with WINi, in which WINi promote accumulation of alternatively spliced isoforms of MDM4 mRNA in which exon 6 is skipped, driving down MDM4 protein levels.
source: Here, however, we also find that there is a second route of p53 activation at work, in which WINi promote accumulation of alternatively spliced isoforms of MDM4 mRNA in which exon 6 is skipped, driving down MDM4 protein levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the alternative splicing and protein expression data.

claim: Because MDM4 inhibits p53 via proteolysis-independent mechanisms, the findings explain how WINi can induce a robust p53 target gene signature in the absence of frank induction of p53 protein.
source: Because MDM4 inhibits p53 via proteolysis-independent mechanisms (Francoz et al., 2006), these findings explain how WINi can induce a robust p53 target gene signature in the absence of frank induction of p53 protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of MDM4 action, with a citation to Francoz et al., 2006.

claim: The findings point to a dominant role of the MDM4–p53 axis in mediating the response of MLLr cells to WIN site blockade.
source: They also point to a dominant role of the MDM4–p53 axis in mediating the response of MLLr cells to WIN site blockade.
